newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia set for new round in political tug-of-war.
newsitem.headline: Russia set for new round in political tug-of-war.

text.p: The Russian government and its communist opponents face a new round of their intricate parliamentary tug-of-war over economic reforms on Wednesday.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house may discuss a government plan to slash spending in the current year following a massive shortfall in budgeted tax revenue. The day's agenda will be set by party managers early in the morning.
Legislators, who stalled the scheme last month, said the latest talks between government and parliamentary representatives on Tuesday ended with the two sides still some way apart.

Ministers, they said, were willing to scale back the cuts to around 85 trillion roubles ($15 billion) from 108 trillion -- about a fifth of total spending in the 1997 budget. But the Duma was unwilling to accept cuts of more than 55 trillion.

Interfax news agency quoted deputy finance minister Vladimir Petrov as saying the outcome was "still hard to predict" but adding: "The two sides have started to seek compromises...We have moved towards one another."

Talks on the cuts -- a procedure known as "sequestration" -- are part of an intensive round of negotiations this week in which the government is pressing for progress on its reform programme before the Duma begins its summer recess on June 24.

On Tuesday, the Duma rejected a package of bills prepared by the cabinet to cut or scrap most of the welfare benefits which served as a complex safety net under the Soviet system but have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.

On Thursday, deputies are due to debate a new tax code which ministers say is the keystone of their 1998 budget and vital for promoting enterprise and rescuing the public finances. The Duma's budget committee has already recommended rejecting it.
But while the struggle between government and parliament may resemble an all-out trial of strength, each side appears unwilling to push things too far for fear of the consequences.

Ministers have made veiled threats that President Boris Yeltsin, who has vast powers under the constitution, might just dissolve parliament. Opposition legislators have threatened the government with a vote of no confidence.

But the Kremlin knows new elections might return an even less cooperative Duma. And many deputies are reluctant to unseat Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin for fear Yeltsin might appoint a more aggressively reform-minded replacement.
"Everyone seems to realise how high the stakes are and the main thing now is not to overpress," a government official said.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, appointed by Yeltsin in March to spearhead a new round of market reforms, said on Tuesday he felt there was "an understanding of sorts between the government and parliament" and refused to accept the Duma would not approve the tax code on Thursday.

Calling the first reading vote "the issue of issues", he held out a hand of compromise to the Duma, saying ministers could amend the code before a second reading if parliament would only approve it at the first.
"Instead of fighting, let's try to do what we can as human beings together," Chubais told reporters.

Echoing less-than-bellicose comments from communist leaders, Chubais said he still believed the welfare reform package could also be passed before the recess and said the government would not oppose setting up a conciliation committee on that issue.
